extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and readers studying algebraic geometry (users of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, definitions, and practical rules for working with functors represented by schemes, computing fibered products/base change, and understanding fibers and geometric fibers of morphisms. Includes which properties are preserved under base change and how to reduce problems to affine/Noetherian/finitely-presented cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representable functors are Zariski sheaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Morphisms to a scheme X glue: for any scheme Y and open cover {Ui} of Y, the equalizer sequence % hX(Y) → ∏ hX(Ui) ⇉ ∏ hX(Ui ∩ Uj) is exact, so the functor hX is a Zariski sheaf. Being a Zariski sheaf is a necessary condition for a functor to be representable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is proved by observing that a morphism Y → X is determined by its restrictions to an open cover that agree on overlaps. (Remark: this is a sheaf on the big Zariski site.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibered product of functors exists (set-theoretic construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given functors h, h', h'' (contravariant Sch → Sets), define (h ×_{h''} h')(W) = h(W) ×_{h''(W)} h'(W). This defines a fibered product of functors (on objects; one must also define its action on morphisms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction requires only the category structure (works with Sch replaced by any category). It shows that fibered products of functors always exist even without representability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open subfunctor criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A map (natural transformation) h' → h expresses h' as an open subfunctor of h if for every representable functor hX and every map hX → h, the fiber product hX ×_h h' is representable by an open embedding U → X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, in the fibered square with hX, the fiber product should be hU with U → X an open embedding. This extends the notion of open embedding from schemes to contravariant functors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representability via local representability (Key Exercise 9.1.I)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a functor h is a Zariski sheaf and has an open cover by representable functors (i.e., 'is covered by schemes'), then h is representable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gluing of schemes (Exercise 4.4.A) to glue the schemes representing the open subfunctors. This gives a sufficient condition: Zariski sheaf + locally representable => representable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibered product computation reduces to four atomic morphism types
rubrics_metrics.description: To compute fibered products of schemes in practice it suffices to understand four types of morphisms: (1) base change by open embeddings, (2) adding variables (A → A[t]), (3) base change by closed embeddings (quotients), and (4) base change by localization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All morphisms can be built from these operations: adding variables corresponds to polynomial algebras, quotients correspond to imposing relations, and localization corresponds to distinguished opens; use these to compute arbitrary tensor-product style fibered products of affines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base change by open embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: Base change with an open embedding is computed by pulling back the open subset: if Y → Z is an open embedding and ψ: X → Z, then the fibered product is the open subscheme ψ^{-1}(Y) of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was used in proving fibered products of schemes exist; explicit universal property verification shows the pullback is the preimage open subset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding variables (base change by polynomial extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding variables commutes with base change: Spec A[t] is the fibered product of Spec A with Spec B[t] over Spec B when A is a B-algebra (i.e., A[t] ≅ A ⊗_B B[t]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show A[t] satisfies the universal property; this allows handling 'adding variables' when computing tensor products of algebras.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base change by closed embeddings (quotients)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fibered product with a closed subscheme is a closed subscheme of the fibered product in the obvious way; in algebra this corresponds to tensoring and quotienting: A/I_e ≅ A ⊗_B (B/I) for an ideal I ⊂ B and its extension I_e ⊂ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use right-exactness of tensor product and extension of ideals to compute the pullback; consequence: closed embeddings are preserved by base change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base change by localization
rubrics_metrics.description: Fibered product with a localization is the localization of the fibered product: if S ⊂ B is multiplicative and A is a B-algebra, then φ(S)^{-1}A ≅ A ⊗_B S^{-1}B. Localizations are preserved by base change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This covers distinguished opens (B → B_f) and fraction fields, and is useful for computing fibers and local behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed embeddings preserved by base change
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y → Z is a closed embedding and X → Z is arbitrary, then the base change W = X ×_Z Y → X is also a closed embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from the algebraic quotient description and Exercise 9.2.B; geometrically, the fibered product with a closed subscheme yields a closed subscheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open embeddings preserved by base change
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y → Z is an open embedding and X → Z is arbitrary, then the base change X ×_Z Y → X is an open embedding (it is ψ^{-1}(Y)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verified by checking the universal property and explicit description of the preimage open subset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally principal closed subschemes preserved by base change
rubrics_metrics.description: Locally principal closed subschemes (locally cut out by one equation) pull back to locally principal closed subschemes under base change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Exercise 9.4.A for details; follows from how functions/polynomials pull back under ring maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of morphisms preserved under base change (list)
rubrics_metrics.description: The following properties of morphisms are preserved by base change: (a) quasicompact, (b) quasiseparated, (c) affine morphism, (d) finite, (e) integral, (f) locally of finite type, (g) finite type, (h) locally of finite presentation, (i) finite presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a broad principle: 'reasonable' properties of morphisms are preserved by pullback; items (h) and (i) are starred (important) and proven via local algebra manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi-finite morphism preserved by base change (with warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of 'quasi-finite' (finite type + finite fibers) is preserved under base change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: the separate notion 'finite fibers' alone is not preserved by base change (counterexamples like Spec Q over Spec Q losing finiteness under some base changes); use quasi-finite as the stable notion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surjectivity preserved by base change
rubrics_metrics.description: If a morphism is surjective, then any base change of it is surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 9.4.D hints at proofs using field extensions and maximal ideals (and choice) to produce points in the fibered product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injectivity need not be preserved by base change
rubrics_metrics.description: Injectivity of a morphism of schemes is not necessarily preserved by base change (Example: Spec C → Spec R is bijective but loses injectivity after base change by Spec C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pathology motivates considering geometric/separable closures and other fixes discussed later (see §9.5.24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: geometric point and geometric fiber
rubrics_metrics.description: A geometric point of a scheme X is a morphism Spec k → X with k algebraically closed. The geometric fiber of X → Y at such a point is the base change X ×_Y Spec k; geometric fibers are used to define geometrically connected/irreducible/integral/reduced fibers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric points enrich ordinary points by specifying an inclusion of the residue field into an algebraically closed field. (Warning: some sources use 'separably closed' instead of 'algebraically closed'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrically connected/irreducible/integral/reduced fibers
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism has geometrically connected (resp. irreducible, integral, reduced) fibers if all geometric fibers (over algebraically closed fields) have the property. A k-scheme X is geometrically connected/irreducible/etc. if X ×_k Spec K has the property for all algebraically closed K containing k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These notions behave well under base change (Exercise 9.5.B). They rectify failures of ordinary fiberwise properties under base change (examples in §9.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of geometric properties via finite/separable extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Although geometric properties a priori require checking all algebraically closed extensions, failures can already be detected after a finite field extension in many cases; e.g., geometrically integral/connected/reduced can be detected after passing to suitable finite or separable closures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists 12 related statements (Ra–Rd, Ia–Id, Ca–Cd) and shows implications like (Rb)⇒(Ra), (Ib)⇒(Ia), etc.; concludes e.g. 'a k-scheme is geometrically integral iff it remains integral under any field extension.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevalley's theorem for locally finitely presented morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a finitely presented B-algebra (not necessarily Noetherian), then the image of Spec A → Spec B is a finite union of locally closed subsets. More generally, for a quasicompact locally finitely presented morphism π: X → Y with Y quasicompact, π(X) is a finite union of locally closed subsets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 9.3.I gives an affine proof using reduction to the Noetherian case via Exercise 9.3.H (express finitely presented morphisms locally as pullbacks of finite type morphisms to a Noetherian scheme).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finitely presented morphisms are locally pullbacks of Noetherian finite-type morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Any finitely presented morphism Spec B ← X is, locally on the base, the pullback of a finitely presented (finite type over Noetherian) morphism Spec Z[x1,...,xN] ← X'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 9.3.H: reduce to the affine case A = B[y1,...,yn]/(f1,...,fr), choose coefficient variables xi, and express X as base change from a Noetherian target. Consequence: results proved for Noetherian schemes and stable under base change apply to finitely presented morphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monomorphisms of schemes: important types
rubrics_metrics.description: Open embeddings, closed embeddings, and localizations of affine schemes are monomorphisms. Monomorphisms are closed under composition, so compositions (e.g., locally closed embeddings, maps from Spec of stalks) are also monomorphisms. Note: Spec O_{X,p} → X is a monomorphism but not generally an open embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 9.2.G asks to show these are monomorphisms using basic properties; be cautious about subtle examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibers and scheme-theoretic fiber computation
rubrics_metrics.description: The fiber of a morphism Y → Z over a point p with residue field K (map Spec K → Z) is the base change Y ×_Z Spec K and can be computed by localization and quotient in affine charts (Ap/pAp etc.). The underlying topological space of the scheme-theoretic fiber agrees with the usual topological fiber.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use affine opens containing the point to reduce to ring-theoretic computations. Exercises 9.3.A–9.3.C and 9.3.B give explicit verifications and analogies with topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite morphisms have finite fibers
rubrics_metrics.description: If a morphism is finite then its fibers are finite (as sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a standard fact (see Exercise 7.3.K) and is recalled here as a useful immediate property when reasoning about fibers.
